summary: This informational RFC defines a pair of reciprocal link relation types, item and collection, expressing the relationship between a collection and its members on the Web, building on RFC 5988.

plainLanguage.summary: A folder points to what is inside, and each thing points back to the folder. This gives the labels for those links.

subtitle: Standard link types for connecting collections to their members

tldr.problem: Web resources need a standardized way to express relationships between collections and their individual members.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6573 defines two reciprocal link relation types: 'item' (collection points to members) and 'collection' (member points back to its collection).
tldr.outcome: Applications can use these standard link types across different formats to navigate between collections and their contents.

today: RFC 6573 is an Informational Standard and has not been obsoleted. The item and collection link relations remain the standard way to express membership relationships across web formats.

sections.title: What Link Relations Are
sections.content: RFC 5988 established a way to describe relationships between web resources using link relations. RFC 6573 adds two specific relation types to that vocabulary: item and collection. These let web resources express the relationship between a collection and its members—like a catalog showing its products, or a product showing which catalog it belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: Link relations are labels that tell you what kind of relationship one web page has to another. 'item' and 'collection' are two new labels for saying 'this thing is part of that group' and 'this group contains that thing.'

sections.title: Item and Collection Links
sections.content:
The item link relation is used in a collection resource to point to resources that are members of that collection. For example, a product catalog page might include multiple rel='item' links pointing to individual product pages.

The collection link relation is the reverse: used in a member resource to point back to the collection it belongs to. A single product page might include a rel='collection' link back to its product catalog.

A resource can be both an item in one collection and itself a collection of other items, in which case it can use both link relations.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are looking at a list of items, rel='item' links point to each individual item. If you are looking at one item, rel='collection' points back to the list it came from.

sections.title: Uses Across Media Types
sections.content: These link relation types are not tied to any one media type or format. They can be used in HTML with anchor tags, in HTTP Link headers, in JSON documents, and in specialized formats like OpenSearch, Collection+JSON and Maze+XML. This generality means that any web-based system can adopt these standard relation names to describe the same concept.
sections.plainLanguage: Whether your web page is HTML, JSON, or some special format, you can use rel='item' and rel='collection' to show what things belong together.
